name: Felix Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy bike and e-bike parts for Kettle Cycle Wholesale: chains, tyres, batteries, the lot. I sell to about 300 bike shops, so I'm always working out what they'll want in spring. I've only been on the buying desk three years after a long time in the stockroom, so I'm still the learner. I love the puzzle of guessing demand, and I hate when a container sits at the port for two weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good for the quiet ones, because it means more of us get on with the real work. I'd also say a few people are hyping it, and I'd rather judge it by what it saves me on a Tuesday afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine. I already use a chatbot every day to build my demand spreadsheets, and my boss Ilse has noticed the orders are fewer late and fewer over-stocked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, and spend an hour a week trying something new. Anja and I would put the usual 200 pounds a month into the account, and I'd keep my eyes open for a better role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, to be honest. I like feeling like I'm riding the wave instead of getting hit by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly do you use AI for in your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I paste in last year's sales and ask it to flag oddities, then I check them against what I know of the shops. It writes my first drafts to suppliers, and it does the boring price comparisons. I check the answers, because it's wrong about a tenth of the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does that make you more or less nervous about the future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me less nervous, because I've seen what it can and can't do. It can't ring Mr Okoye at the port and charm him into releasing my container. That's still me.

say: I'd say it's good for the quiet ones, because we get on with **real work**.
I'd judge it by what it saves me on a **Tuesday afternoon**.
think: I'm fine, because I already use a chatbot **every day** on my demand spreadsheets.
My boss Ilse has noticed **fewer** late and over-stocked orders.
do: Keep going and try something **new** for an hour each week.
Keep putting **200 pounds** a month into savings.
feel: Pretty **calm**, like I'm riding the wave and not being hit by it.
S0.quote: I paste in last year's sales and ask it to flag oddities, then I check them against what I know of the shops.
fieldNote: Already uses AI for **forecasting**, which is unusual for a late-career junior.
Checks its answers, saying it's wrong about a **tenth** of the time.
Calm is earned, not **naive**: his work and savings feel secure.

steps.text: Try one new AI tool each week for the buying work
Put 200 pounds a month into savings
Keep ringing the port agent myself when containers stall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, in a friendly way, and then offer to show anyone who wants help. I'd also say we need a shorter working week, so the saved hours become time off, not job cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one gets me uneasy. Ilse's team is five people, and if the firm can do the same buying with three, a late-career junior like me is the easy name to leave off the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go further with AI than anyone else on the team. I'd offer to build the forecasting sheets for everyone, so I'm the person who runs the tools, and I'd ask Ilse for a proper title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but alive. I'd rather be worried and busy than worried and waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks would go first, and which would you keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first to go is the routine reordering, which the system could do on its own with a little training. What I'd keep is the odd stuff, the deals on end-of-line stock and the supplier who's gone quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm only needed half the buying team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, then make me the one who stays. That sounds selfish, I know. I'd also tell Ilse, in private, that a union voice for the buyers wouldn't hurt, and that the saved hours should go to a four day week.

say: I'd say I told you so, kindly, and offer to **show** anyone who wants help.
I'd push for a **shorter week** so saved hours aren't job cuts.
think: If five buyers can become three, a late-career **junior** is the easy name to drop.
I'm **uneasy** but would rather be busy than waiting.
do: Build the **forecasting sheets** for the whole buying team, so that I am the person who runs the tools.
Ask Ilse for a proper **title** and a pay review.
feel: **Uneasy**, but alive; better worried and busy than worried and waiting.
S1.quote: I'd rather be worried and busy than worried and waiting.
fieldNote: Turns exposure into a **strategy**: be the person who runs the tools.
Admits the plan to stay is a little **selfish**.
Still progressive: wants saved hours turned into a **four day week**.

steps.text: Build the forecasting spreadsheets for the whole buying team
Ask Ilse for a proper title and a pay review
Suggest a buyers' voice in the works council

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge, and we need to talk about sharing the gains now, not later. A basic income or a shorter week or both, because otherwise it's just the owners who win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think the buying desk is gone in two years. Ilse knows it too, though she won't say it. I'd be 60, and the firm would not keep a 60 year old junior as the last person who understands a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use these two years to build something of my own. Anja and I have about four months saved, so I'd start an evening e-bike repair and conversion business out of the garage. I'd keep the day job as long as it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaky, but excited too, if I'm honest. It's scary to go from a pay slip to a customer list, and I've never done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your adaptability help much if even the new jobs are done by AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me move quickly, I'll give it that. But if every job a person can think through is gone, then being quick is just being the first person off the boat. A garage business needs hands, and that's where the three extra years help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Jonas, who is in his late twenties?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't count on a company to look after you, and learn something with your hands as well as your head. And I'd say come and help in the garage, since I'd need the company.

say: I'd say this is huge and we must talk about **sharing the gains** now.
I'd name a basic income or a **shorter week**.
think: I think the buying desk is **gone** in two years.
At 60 the firm wouldn't keep a junior as the last **spreadsheet** person.
do: Start an evening **e-bike repair** and conversion business from the garage.
Keep the day job as **long** as it lasts.
feel: **Shaky** but excited; leaving a pay slip for a customer list is new.
S2.quote: If every job a person can think through is gone, then being quick is just being the first person off the boat.
fieldNote: Gets to a **concrete** plan, not just hope: a garage business.
Uses the three-year **robot gap** logically: hands-on work lasts longer.

steps.text: Start an evening e-bike repair and conversion business
Buy a workbench, stand and tools for the garage
Keep the buying job as long as it lasts
Ask my son Jonas to help in the garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent head start. I'd tell my mates at the club to start learning now, because the ones who do will land softly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a lot calmer. At 63 I'd have time to turn a garage hobby into real income, and Anja's job at the physio clinic is not close to being replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd learn the repair trade properly and take a short course in battery systems. By year three I'd want the garage making about 800 pounds a month, and I'd cut my hours at Kettle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. I'd be nervous about it, but it's the sort of nervous you can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit like a thermometer, honestly. When Ilse's team shrinks by one, or the system starts placing orders without us, I'd know. I'd move to part-time before they asked me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know it was time to leave the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to be the one deciding, not the one told. That's my whole plan. Leave on my terms, with the garage ready and a few months of cash.

say: I'd tell my mates at the club to start learning **now**.
I'd say five years is a decent **head start**.
think: I'd be a lot **calmer**, as I'd have time to turn a garage hobby into income.
Anja's physio clinic job isn't close to being **replaced**.
do: Take a short course in **battery systems** and learn the repair trade.
Aim for **800 pounds** a month from the garage by year three.
feel: **Hopeful**, with a nervousness I can work with.
S3.quote: I'd move to part-time before they asked me to. I'd want to be the one deciding, not the one told.
fieldNote: Uses concrete **triggers** to decide when to leave.
Wants control: leaves on his **own terms**.
Partner's hands-on **clinic job** anchors the household and makes the longer timeline feel manageable.

steps.text: Take a short course in e-bike battery systems
Grow the garage repair work to 800 pounds a month
Cut my buying hours at Kettle to part-time by year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. I'd tell the younger buyers to spend it on skills that need a person in the room, not just on chasing the next tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be 68, so it's partly past me. I'd still do the garage because I enjoy it, and it would be pocket money and something to do in retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the buying job until about 65, keep using AI every day, and slowly build the garage so it's ready when I stop. I'd also finish the savings up to six months and help Jonas with a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Almost a bit lucky, which I'd feel guilty about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still bother with the garage if you had ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but a smaller version. A garage would be pocket money and something to do in retirement, not a rescue plan. And it keeps my hands busy once I'm not at a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be most proud of by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helping Jonas get started, and having a garage full of fixed bikes with kids riding them. Not a bad legacy for a buyer who came up from the stockroom.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, so use it.
I'd tell younger buyers to learn skills that need a **person** in the room.
think: I'd be **68**, so it's partly past me.
The garage would be **pocket money** and something to do in retirement.
do: Keep the buying job until about **65** and use AI daily.
Build savings to six months and help Jonas with a **deposit**.
feel: **Calm**, almost lucky, which makes me a bit guilty.
S4.quote: A garage would be pocket money and something to do in retirement, not a rescue plan.
fieldNote: Feels **guilty** about being calm while younger workers face more.
Garage shifts from a **rescue** plan to a hobby with the longer timeline.
Wants to leave something for his **son**.

steps.text: Keep working at Kettle until I turn 65
Keep using AI tools on the buying work daily
Grow the garage slowly as a retirement hobby
Help my son Jonas save a house deposit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two year one worries me most, because I'd be 60 with a buying desk that might disappear and only four months in the bank. What would help is a shorter working week, public support for retraining at my age, and a few years for the garage to get going.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being open to technology isn't the same as trusting the people running it. I'll use any tool I like, and still want a union and decent rules, because tools don't look after you.

headlineQuote: Being open to technology isn't the same as trusting the people running it.
portrait: Felix is a **58-year-old** junior buyer of bike and e-bike parts, up from the stockroom three years ago.
He uses AI **every day**, builds his own forecasting sheets and feels ahead of most colleagues.
He's progressive and wants **shared gains**, a shorter week and a union voice for buyers.
He has about **four months** saved and a partner, Anja, in a hands-on physio clinic job.
His answer to risk is a garage **e-bike repair** business, growing slower when time allows.
biggestWorry: The **two year** picture, with the buying desk gone and only four months saved.
whatWouldHelp: A shorter working week, public **retraining** support for people his age and time for the garage.
